MANDATORY SINGLE-MODEL EXPERIMENT: train one independent model per category.
Do not implement ensembles, bagging, boosting of independent predictors, stacking,
multi-seed/checkpoint averaging, score/rank voting, mixtures of independently fitted
experts, or neural scores combined with separately fitted transition/popularity scores.
Each category must load exactly one independently trained model/checkpoint at prediction.
Jointly trained internal layers/features of one network are allowed. Four category
models are necessary for routing and do not constitute an ensemble. All hypotheses,
code generation, debugging, reviews and memory use must respect this constraint even
if an upstream generic prompt suggests an ensemble. The host audits the actual
predictor before accepting validation scores; violations fail the trial and consume
their training budget. Do not read other trials or reuse their trained checkpoints.

 ## Search results
Closest direct match: [HSTU-BLaIR (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10545) enriches HSTU item representations with textual metadata embeddings and reports improvements on two Amazon Reviews 2023 domains. However, it uses a pretrained BLaIR encoder; its results do not establish that text encoders learned from scratch improve sparse-item ranking. [SimRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.22136v1) provides complementary evidence: title-derived similarity distributions supervise next-item scores through an auxiliary loss, helping rare items without adding inference parameters. Its experiments also use pretrained text embeddings and a SASRec backbone, so transferring the loss to HSTU remains a hypothesis.

A constraint-compatible experiment would retain HSTU and represent each item with an ID embedding plus projected title/description features from a small, randomly initialized token encoder, jointly optimized by next-item training. Shared token embeddings and mean pooling offer a low-cost starting point; ID dropout could encourage content use. These are proposed adaptations, not verified findings from the cited papers. [DenseRec (2025)](https://earl-workshop.github.io/pdf/recsys2025-workshops_paper_167.pdf) supports preserving collaborative identity alongside content, while warning that semantic similarity alone can miss contextual relevance; it likewise relies on pretrained content embeddings. Treat explicit model numbers and compatibility phrases in available text as learnable evidence, never as guaranteed compatibility labels. Validate against ID-only HSTU using the fixed macro HR@10, with training-frequency breakdowns for diagnosis. The located evidence supports testing this single-network design, but does not demonstrate gains under the exact no-pretraining constraint.

HSTU already supports sampled-softmax training: Meta’s released MovieLens configuration uses 128 negatives, temperature 0.05, and normalized user/item embeddings. This supports changing the objective or sampler while retaining HSTU, but does not establish optimal settings for Amazon Electronics. Large margins against easy negatives alone cannot establish ranking generalization. [Official HSTU configuration](https://github.com/meta-recsys/generative-recommenders/blob/main/configs/ml-1m/hstu-sampled-softmax-n128-final.gin)

LogQ correction addresses sampling bias, especially the disproportionate use of popular items as in-batch negatives. The 2025 paper *Correcting the LogQ Correction* identifies an additional distinction: the positive is always included, rather than sampled, and derives a revised correction. Therefore, do not blindly subtract the same logQ term from every logit; correction must match the actual sampling scheme. Hard-negative selection changes that scheme further. [RecSys 2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331)

Practical hypothesis: compare larger uniform-negative sampled softmax against a uniform-plus-moderately-hard objective, mining with the same HSTU network after warm-up. Exclude known training positives and duplicate candidates; retain random negatives rather than selecting only the highest-scoring items. These are proposed ablations, not demonstrated improvements: Hard-BPR finds that hard sampling can amplify false-negative damage and motivates a robust objective. Unknown relevance remains unknown; high scores do not prove negative labels. Keep one model per category, fixed seeds and training limits, and select by the prescribed four-category macro validation HR@10, examining Electronics separately. [Hard-BPR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19276)

HSTU (2024) combines relative position/time attention bias, pointwise SiLU attention aggregation, and multiplicative gating. These mechanisms support learning time-sensitive dependencies, but its gate does not explicitly identify short-term intent or completed needs. Relative temporal bias provides a natural place to model elapsed-time effects while preserving the HSTU backbone. [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152).

Later research supports distinguishing persistent preferences from recent activity. “Don’t Waste It” (2025) introduces jointly trained, prior-conditioned adapter heads for interpretable dimensions including long- versus short-term interests. Rec2PM (2026) compresses histories into preference-memory tokens, reporting denoising and robust long-term-interest retention. HPGR (2026) explicitly models session structure and uses preference-guided sparse attention to select relevant history. These offer related design evidence, without establishing that recency alone identifies the user’s current task. [Temporal priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10492), [Rec2PM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11605), [HPGR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00980).
